name: Dispatch
markdown:
# `Dispatch`

Make a new method function

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Dispatch`  

## Description

The code above creates a method function that takes up to four arguments, looking up the appropriate method according to the classes of the arguments, with inheritance.  To install a method for two arguments, (x, y), of classes X and Y, use code like this:     f(X, Y) := (x, y) -> ...where '...' represents the body of the function you wish to install. The syntax for one or three arguments is analogous.  See [:=](../../Core/operator/_col__eq_.md) for details. In the following example we install a asymmetric method to illustrate the left-associative order of evaluation for a binary method function. By default, at most four arguments (in a sequence) can be handled by a method function, and the types have to be considered separately when installing methods. In this example, we define a method function that treats a sequence as a single argument, and we install a method for handling such arguments. Here we define a method whose first argument is to be a type.  It will convert its second argument to that type. In the next example we make a linear function of a single real variable whose coefficients are provided as optional arguments named Slope and Intercept, with default value 1. The methods installed for this method function should be written in the form `opts -> args -> (...)`.  The argument `opts` will be assigned a hash table of type [OptionTable](../../Core/type/OptionTable.md) containing the optional argument names and their current values.  For example, in the body of the function, the current value for the argument named `b` can be recovered with `opts#b`, or with `opts.b`, in case `b` is known to be a global symbol.  Be careful not to change the value of `b`, or the code will stop working; it would be a good idea to protect it. The default [OptionTable](../../Core/type/OptionTable.md) for `r` can be recovered with the function [options](../../Core/function/options.md).  The options given to [method](../../Core/function/method.md) can be recovered with [methodOptions](../../Core/function/methodOptions.md). In the next example we define a method function that leaves option processing to the individual methods. For now, one installs a method function for `s` with no non-optional arguments using [installMethod](../../Core/function/installMethod.md):### Functions with optional argument named Dispatch: For the programmerThe object [Dispatch](../../Core/object/Dispatch.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).

name: Down
markdown:
# `Down`

Monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Down`  

## Description

`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see `monomial_spc_orderings`. Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/object/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/object/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/object/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/object/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/object/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/object/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/object/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.


## Examples

```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```
```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```
```macaulay2
x<1
```
```
o2 = true
```
```macaulay2
y<1
```
```
o3 = false
```

name: except
markdown:
# `except`

Catch an error

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$except`  

## Description

The return value is the value returned by y or z, as the case may be. The clause `then y` may be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by x if there is no error or alarm. The clause `else z` may be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by y, unless an error or alarm occurs, in which case [null](../../Core/object/null.md) is returned. The clauses `then y else z` may both be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by x, unless an error or alarm occurs, in which case [null](../../Core/object/null.md) is returned. In the alternate form `try x then y except err do z`, x is first evaluated. If no error occurs, then the value of y is returned, or the value of x if the `then y` clause is omitted. If an error occurs, then the corresponding [Error](../../Core/type/Error.md) object is assigned to the symbol specified by err. That symbol is then available during the evaluation of z, whose value is returned. The behavior of interrupts (other than alarms) is unaffected.### CaveatWe will change the behavior of this function soon so that it will be possible to catch errors of a particular type.  Meanwhile, users are recommended to use this function sparingly, if at all.


## Examples

```macaulay2
apply(-3..3, i -> try 1/i then 1/i else infinity)
```

name: for
markdown:
# `for`

For loops

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$for`  

## Description

ExamplesThe expressions in this construction may be arbitrarily complicated. Here is an example where `z` is a sequence of expressions separated by semicolons (see [;](../../Core/operator/_scol_.md)). The `do z` clause may be omitted. The `from m` clause may be omitted, in which case `i` starts with `0`. The `when p` clause may be omitted. The `to n` clause may be omitted. The `list x` clause may be omitted. If [continue](../../Core/object/continue.md) is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, no value is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `continue w` is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, the value of `w` is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `break v` is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and `v` is returned as its value. If [break](../../Core/object/break.md) is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and the list accumulated so far is returned as the value. If `v` is an instance of any class with the [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) method installed (e.g., a string), then the values of `i` are obtained by repeatedly calling [next](../../Core/function/next.md) on the output of `iterator v` until [StopIteration](../../Core/object/StopIteration.md) is returned.### CaveatThe variable `i` is a new local variable whose scope includes only the expressions `p`, `x`, and `z` in the body of the loop.  Moreover, new local variables defined inside the body of the loop will not be visible outside it.


## Examples

```macaulay2
for i from 1 to 5 when i < 15 list i^2 do print i
1
2
3
4
5
```

```
o1 = {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}
o1 : List
```

```
o2 : List
```

```macaulay2
print "The value of i is : ";
print i
)
```

name: gbTrace
markdown:
# `gbTrace`

Current engine computation tracing level

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** ZZ  
**Aliases:** `Core$gbTrace`  

## Description

`gbTrace = n` -- set the tracing level for `the_spc_engine_spc_of_spc_Macaulay2` to level `n`.  Meaningful values of `n` for typical users are 0, 1, 2, and 3.  Meaningful values for the developers are 4, 5, 8, 10, 11, and 100; the parity also has an effect when the value is at least 5. The notations used in tracing are: g       - a generator reduced to something nonzero and has been added to the basis.m       - an S-pair reduced to something nonzero and has been added to the basis.z       - an S-pair reduced to zero, and a syzygy has been recorded.u       - an S-pair reduced to zero, but the syzygy need not be recorded.o       - an S-pair or generator reduced to zero, but no new syzygy occurred.r       - an S-pair has been removed.{2}     - beginning to reduce the S-pairs of degree 2.(7)     - 7 more S-pairs need to be reduced.(8,9)   - 9 S-pairs, 8 predicted basis elements (`gb_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_Hilbert_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_`).       - a minor has been computed, or something has happened while computing a resolution.

name: Global
markdown:
# `Global`

Monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Global`  

## Description

`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see `monomial_spc_orderings`. Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/object/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/object/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/object/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/object/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/object/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/object/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/object/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.### Functions with optional argument named Global: For the programmerThe object [Global](../../Core/object/Global.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).


## Examples

```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```
```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```
```macaulay2
x<1
```
```
o2 = true
```
```macaulay2
y<1
```
```
o3 = false
```

- `grevlexWeight`
- `monomial_spc_orderings`
- `weightGrevlex`

name: GRevLex
markdown:
# `GRevLex`

Graded reverse lexicographical monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$GRevLex`  

## Description

The graded reverse lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if either $degree(x^A) > degree(x^B)$ or $degree(x^A) = degree(x^B)$ and the LAST non-zero entry of the vector of integers $A-B$ is NEGATIVE. This is the default order in Macaulay2, in large part because it is often the most efficient order for use with Gröbner bases.  By giving GRevLex a list of integers, one may change the definition of the order: $degree(x^A)$ is the dot product of $A$ with the argument of GRevLex. The largest possible exponent of variables in the `GRevLex` order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, it is sometimes useful to limit the size of monomials (this often makes computations more efficient). Use `MonomialSize => 16`, which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or `MonomialSize => 8`, which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1.


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d];
```
```macaulay2
a^3 + b^2 + b*c
3    2
```
```
o2 = a  + b  + b*c
o2 : R
```
```macaulay2
S = QQ[a..d, MonomialOrder => GRevLex => {1,2,3,4}];
```
```macaulay2
a^3 + b^2 + b*c
2    3
```
```
o4 = b*c + b  + a
o4 : S
```
```macaulay2
B1 = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16,MonomialOrder=>GRevLex];
```
```macaulay2
B = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16];
```
```macaulay2
a^(2^15-1)
32767
```
```
o7 = a
o7 : B
```
```macaulay2
C = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>8,MonomialOrder=>GRevLex];
```
```macaulay2
try a^(2^15-1) else "failed"
```
```
o9 = failed
```
```macaulay2
a^(2^7-1)
127
```
```
o10 = a
o10 : C
```
## See also

- `packing_spc_monomials_spc_for_spc_efficiency`

name: in
markdown:
# `in`

For loops

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$in`  

## Description

ExamplesThe expressions in this construction may be arbitrarily complicated. Here is an example where `z` is a sequence of expressions separated by semicolons (see [;](../../Core/operator/_scol_.md)). The `do z` clause may be omitted. The `from m` clause may be omitted, in which case `i` starts with `0`. The `when p` clause may be omitted. The `to n` clause may be omitted. The `list x` clause may be omitted. If [continue](../../Core/object/continue.md) is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, no value is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `continue w` is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, the value of `w` is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `break v` is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and `v` is returned as its value. If [break](../../Core/object/break.md) is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and the list accumulated so far is returned as the value. If `v` is an instance of any class with the [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) method installed (e.g., a string), then the values of `i` are obtained by repeatedly calling [next](../../Core/function/next.md) on the output of `iterator v` until [StopIteration](../../Core/object/StopIteration.md) is returned.### CaveatThe variable `i` is a new local variable whose scope includes only the expressions `p`, `x`, and `z` in the body of the loop.  Moreover, new local variables defined inside the body of the loop will not be visible outside it.

## Description

The document key is the name of the node, specifically the one that allows users to find the documentation for the desired command. Some node names, rather than being strings, are sequences of Macaulay2 objects that refer to specific method functions. If one is documenting a function of Macaulay2, the key will just be the function's name, as in the documentation for `resolution`. However, if one is documenting a method for a function, then the key will have a different form, as in the documentation for `resolution_lpar_Module_rpar_`. If one is documenting an optional argument to a function, then the key has a different form still, as in `resolution_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_SyzygyLimit_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_`. Finally, if one is documenting an overview of a group of functions or a package, as in `ideals` then one would set up a document key of the form:### CaveatNo two documentation nodes may have the same key or even a key that is a synonym for a key which is already used. However, sometimes there is a need for several documentation nodes to have the same key. This happens when a command that needs to be documented is a synonym for another already documented command. In this case the synonym's key should be stated in quotation marks. name: Layout
markdown:
# `Layout`

Relative locations of Macaulay2 files

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** HashTable  
**Aliases:** `Core$Layout`  

## Description

Macaulay2 comes with a variety of types of files, and some of them are associated with a particular Macaulay2 package.  The hash table `currentLayout` is a translation table from names, corresponding to the various types of files, to directory paths.  The directory paths are to be interpreted relative to the path stored in [prefixDirectory](../../Core/object/prefixDirectory.md).  Each of the directories contained in the list [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) has its own layout, which will be detected at runtime. Some of the strings contain `PKG` as a substring, which should be replaced by the name of package whose files will be stored in that directory. The hash table [Layout](../../Core/object/Layout.md) contains the two possible values for [currentLayout](../../Core/object/currentLayout.md); corresponding to the two possible values for the `installPackage_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_SeparateExec_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_` option used with [installPackage](../../Core/function/installPackage.md). The hash table `Layout#2` is used if architecture dependent files are to be stored in a directory tree separate from the one used for architecture independent files.  The hash table `Layout#1` is used otherwise. Basic Macaulay2 files are regarded as being associated with a special package called `Core`, and the corresponding documentation files are part of the package `Macaulay2Doc`. Here are the meanings of the keys used in [currentLayout](../../Core/object/currentLayout.md).`"bin"` : executable files (M2)`"data"` : architecture independent data files`"docdir"` : documentation for Macaulay2 packages`"emacs"` : Emacs source files (*.el, *.elc)`"factory gftables"` : directory for files containing addition tables in small finite fields used by the library 'factory'`"info"` : documentation in info form`"lib"` : architecture dependent data and executable files`"libraries"` : dynamically loadable libraries from third party packages linked with Macaulay2`"man"` : man pages`"package"` : additional source files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagecache"` : cached data files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagedoc"` : documentation for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packageexampleoutput"` : example output files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packagehtml"` : html documentation for the Macaulay2 package PKG (*.html)`"packagelib"` : architecture dependent files for the Macaulay2 package PKG`"packages"` : source files for Macaulay2 packages; this directory appears on the path`"program licenses"` : licenses for programs to be run by Macaulay2`"programs"` : programs to be run by Macaulay2

name: Lex
markdown:
# `Lex`

Lexicographical monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Lex`  

## Description

The lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if the FIRST non-zero entry of the vector of integers `A-B` is POSITIVE. The largest possible exponent of variables in `Lex` order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, the size of the exponents of variables may be restricted.  Then instead of `Lex`, one can use ` MonomialSize=>16`, which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or `MonomialSize=>8`, which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1. Any of these versions of `Lex` order may be combined, for example, with a weight order given by a weight vector: x^A > x^B if weight(x^A) > weight(x^B) or if weight(x^A) = weight(x^B) and if the FIRST non-zero entry of the vector of integers A-B is POSITIVE.


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d, MonomialOrder => Lex];
```
```macaulay2
a^3 + a^2*b^2 + b*c
3    2 2
```
```
o2 = a  + a b  + b*c
o2 : R
```
```macaulay2
B = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>Lex,MonomialSize=>16];
```
```macaulay2
a^(2^15-1)
32767
```
```
o4 = a
o4 : B
```
```macaulay2
C = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>Lex,MonomialSize=>8];
```
```macaulay2
try a^(2^15-1) else "failed"
```
```
o6 = failed
```
```macaulay2
a^(2^7-1)
127
```
```
o7 = a
o7 : C
```
```macaulay2
B = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2,3,4}, Lex}];
```
```macaulay2
a^2 + b+ c + b*d
2
```
```
o9 = b*d + c + a  + b
o9 : B
```
## See also

- [Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md)

markdown:
# `loadDepth`

The load depth

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** ZZ  
**Aliases:** `Core$loadDepth`  

## Description

`loadDepth = i` -- sets the load depth to `i`, which should be a small integer, returning the old value. During the backtrace after an error message, a position in interpreted code is displayed only if the load depth at the time the code was parsed is at least as large as the error depth is now.  The load depth is set to 0 initially, is set to 1 when the files of the [Core](../../Core/package/Core.md) package are being loaded, is set to 2 while loading a package with the [debuggingMode](../../Core/object/debuggingMode.md) option set to [false](../../Core/object/false.md), and is set to 3 while loading a package with the [debuggingMode](../../Core/object/debuggingMode.md) option set to [true](../../Core/object/true.md) and for user input. The value of [loadDepth](../../Core/object/loadDepth.md) active when code is parsed is referred to later when error messages are being handled: see [errorDepth](../../Core/object/errorDepth.md), and it is also displayed, in parentheses, when the error message is printed.### CaveatThe user should not attempt to adjust the value of [loadDepth](../../Core/object/loadDepth.md).

name: minimalPresentationMap
markdown:
# `minimalPresentationMap`

Compute a minimal presentation of a quotient ring

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$minimalPresentationMap`  

## Description

The computation is accomplished by considering the relations of `R`. If a variable occurs as a term of a relation of `R` and in no other terms of the same polynomial, then  the variable is replaced by the remaining terms and removed from the ring.  A minimal generating set for the resulting defining ideal is then computed and the new quotient ring is returned. If `R` is not homogeneous, then an attempt is made to improve the presentation. If the Exclude option is present, then those variables with the given indices are not simplified away (remember that ring variable indices start at 0).


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = ZZ/101[x,y,z,u,w]/ideal(x-x^2-y,z+x*y,w^2-u^2);
```
```macaulay2
minimalPresentation(R)
ZZ
---[x, u, w]
101
```
```
o2 = ------------
2    2
- u  + w
o2 : QuotientRing
```
```macaulay2
R.minimalPresentationMap
ZZ
---[x, u, w]
101                     2       3    2
```
```
o3 = map (------------, R, {x, - x  + x, x  - x , u, w})
2    2
- u  + w
ZZ
---[x, u, w]
101
o3 : RingMap ------------ <-- R
2    2
- u  + w
```
```macaulay2
R.minimalPresentationMapInv
ZZ
---[x, u, w]
101
```
```
o4 = map (R, ------------, {x, u, w})
2    2
- u  + w
ZZ
---[x, u, w]
101
o4 : RingMap R <-- ------------
2    2
- u  + w
```
```macaulay2
R = ZZ/101[x,y,z,u,w]/ideal(x-x^2-y,z+x*y,w^2-u^2);
```
```macaulay2
minimalPresentation(R, Exclude=>{1})
ZZ
---[x..y, u, w]
101
```
```
o6 = -------------------------
2             2    2
(- x  + x - y, - u  + w )
o6 : QuotientRing
```

name: MonomialOrder
markdown:
# `MonomialOrder`

Monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$MonomialOrder`  

## Description

`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see `monomial_spc_orderings`. Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/object/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/object/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/object/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/object/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/object/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/object/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/object/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.### Functions with optional argument named MonomialOrder: For the programmerThe object [MonomialOrder](../../Core/object/MonomialOrder.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).


## Examples

```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```
```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```
```macaulay2
x<1
```
```
o2 = true
```
```macaulay2
y<1
```
```
o3 = false
```

The dictionaries for the symbols in the packages loaded by the user are moved out of the way to avoid conflicts, so just the standard pre-loaded packages are visible to the source code of the package.  In addition, the package `SimpleDoc` is made available. If functions from additional packages are needed by the code in the new package, then [needsPackage](../../Core/function/needsPackage.md) can be used (after the use of `newPackage`) to provide them. If functions from additional packages are needed by the user who will load the new package, then [needsPackage](../../Core/function/needsPackage.md) can be used (before the use of `newPackage`) to provide them. The options can be recovered with [options](../../Core/function/options.md) as follows. Here is a template for a typical `newPackage` entry in a package.### Functions with optional argument named Name: For the programmerThe object [Name](../../Core/object/Name.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).

name: newline
markdown:
# `newline`

The new line character sequence

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** String  
**Aliases:** `Core$newline`  

## Description

`newline` -- a string containing the character or sequence of characters that represents the end of a line.  To end an output line, you should use [endl](../../Core/function/endl.md) instead, because there is more to ending an output line than emitting the characters in `newline`, especially when nets are being used. This string depends on what your operating system is: on Unix systems it is the ascii character 10; on Macintoshes it is the ascii character 13, and under MS-DOS and Windows 95 it is a string of length 2 containing ascii characters 13 and 10. Try to avoid confusing the newline string described here with the ASCII character called `newline`.  That character can be incorporated into a string with the escape sequence `\n`, and it always has ASCII code 10.


## Examples

name: numTBBThreads
markdown:
# `numTBBThreads`

Parallelism in engine computations

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** ZZ  
**Aliases:** `Core$numTBBThreads`  

## Description

Some computations in the engine can run using multiple cores on your computer. Currently, this includes computation of minimal betti diagrams, non-minimal resolutions, and Gröbner bases of 2-sided ideals in associative algebras, all in the graded case, over a finite field.  Also included is (one of the algorithms for) the computation of Gröbner bases in polynomial rings over finite fields, whether graded or not. The variable `numTBBThreads` controls the number of cores used by Macaulay2. The default value (zero) means the system can choose an appropriate number of cores (often the maximum available).  Note that the default behavior is to use multiple cores. In [minimalBetti](../../Core/function/minimalBetti.md), and in `freeResolution` with the `Strategy => Nonminimal` option, more aggressive parallelism that sometimes uses a lot of memory but can sometimes produce answers in less time can be enabled using the `ParallelizeByDegree` boolean option. For examples, we show some simple examples of computation which, for larger size problems, might benefit from using parallelism.  Note that in each of these cases, the default is to use all available CPU cores for computation. For these particularly simple examples, the overhead for using multiple cores is non-trivial with respect to the total computation time.  Significant speedup is achieved when the time to gauss reduce the requisite matrices is large compared to creating these matrices. Gröbner bases (based on a linear algebra method, e.g. Faugere's F4 algorithm, are also parallelized.  Note: the MGB Strategy of groebnerBasis is not currently parallelized. For Gröbner basis computation in associative algebras, `ParallelizeByDegree` is not relevant.  In this case, use `numTBBThreads` to control the amount of parallelism.

name: ParallelizeByDegree
markdown:
# `ParallelizeByDegree`

Parallelism in engine computations

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$ParallelizeByDegree`  

## Description

Some computations in the engine can run using multiple cores on your computer. Currently, this includes computation of minimal betti diagrams, non-minimal resolutions, and Gröbner bases of 2-sided ideals in associative algebras, all in the graded case, over a finite field.  Also included is (one of the algorithms for) the computation of Gröbner bases in polynomial rings over finite fields, whether graded or not. The variable `numTBBThreads` controls the number of cores used by Macaulay2. The default value (zero) means the system can choose an appropriate number of cores (often the maximum available).  Note that the default behavior is to use multiple cores. In [minimalBetti](../../Core/function/minimalBetti.md), and in `freeResolution` with the `Strategy => Nonminimal` option, more aggressive parallelism that sometimes uses a lot of memory but can sometimes produce answers in less time can be enabled using the `ParallelizeByDegree` boolean option. For examples, we show some simple examples of computation which, for larger size problems, might benefit from using parallelism.  Note that in each of these cases, the default is to use all available CPU cores for computation. For these particularly simple examples, the overhead for using multiple cores is non-trivial with respect to the total computation time.  Significant speedup is achieved when the time to gauss reduce the requisite matrices is large compared to creating these matrices. Gröbner bases (based on a linear algebra method, e.g. Faugere's F4 algorithm, are also parallelized.  Note: the MGB Strategy of groebnerBasis is not currently parallelized. For Gröbner basis computation in associative algebras, `ParallelizeByDegree` is not relevant.  In this case, use `numTBBThreads` to control the amount of parallelism.### Functions with optional argument named ParallelizeByDegree: For the programmerThe object [ParallelizeByDegree](../../Core/object/ParallelizeByDegree.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).

# `Position`

Monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Position`  

## Description

`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see `monomial_spc_orderings`. name: POSIX
markdown: # `POSIX` Evaluate a regular expression search **Package:** Core **Class:** Symbol **Aliases:** `Core$POSIX` ## Description The value returned is a list of pairs of integers corresponding to the parenthesized subexpressions successfully matched, suitable for use as the first argument of [substring](../../Core/function/substring.md). The first member of each pair is the offset within `str` of the substring matched, and the second is the length. See `regular_spc_expressions` for a brief introduction to the topic. By default, the regular expressions are interpreted using the Perl flavor, which supports features such as lookaheads and lookbehinds for fine-tuning the matches. This syntax is used in Perl and JavaScript languages. Alternatively, one can choose the POSIX Extended flavor of regex using `POSIX => true`. This syntax is similar to the one used by the Unix utilities `egrep` and `awk` and enforces the leftmost, longest rule for finding matches. If there's a tie, the rule is applied to the first subexpression. In the Perl flavor, one can specify whether repetitions should be possessive or non-greedy.### Functions with optional argument named POSIX: For the programmerThe object [POSIX](../../Core/object/POSIX.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md). ## Examples ```macaulay2 s = "The cat is black."; name: prefixDirectory
markdown:
# `prefixDirectory`

The prefix directory

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** String  
**Aliases:** `Core$prefixDirectory`  

## Description

When Macaulay2 is successfully installed, its files are installed in a directory tree whose layout, relative to the root, is determined by the hash table [Layout](../../Core/object/Layout.md).  When M2 starts up, it detects whether it is running in such a layout, and sets [prefixDirectory](../../Core/object/prefixDirectory.md) to the root of that directory tree.  The way it does that is that it locates the running M2 executable and determines whether it is located in a directory whose name is `bin` that has a sibling directory called `share` that leads to a directory called `share/Macaulay2/Core/`. The prefix directory can be set by the user at an early stage when `M2` starts up with the `--prefix` command line option.  This will affect the value of [path](../../Core/object/path.md) and thus the locations of the files loaded initially.  Use the `--notify` command line option to display the locations of files as they are loaded.

## See also

- `invoking_spc_the_spc_Macaulay2_spc_program`
- [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md)

name: prefixPath
markdown:
# `prefixPath`

Absolute locations of Macaulay2 files

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** List  
**Aliases:** `Core$prefixPath`  

## Description

The absolute location of a Macaulay2 file can be obtained by concatenating three components: (a) the prefix, which is one of the members of the list [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md); (b) the relative location of the directory containing the file, as recorded in the hash table [Layout](../../Core/object/Layout.md); and (c) the base name of the file. The value of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) is used by [installPackage](../../Core/function/installPackage.md) when determining how to direct documentation hyperlinks from one package to another. The initial value of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) contains just the following two optional items. If the variable [prefixDirectory](../../Core/object/prefixDirectory.md) was given a non-null value initially or by a `-e` command line argument, then it will be the last element of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md).  If the `-q` option was not given on the command line used to invoke Macaulay2, then the value of `applicationDirectory()|"local/"` will be the first element of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md).  No attempt is made to synchronize the value of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) with the values of [prefixDirectory](../../Core/object/prefixDirectory.md) and of `applicationDirectory()`, which may change. When running a newly compiled version of Macaulay2, adding something like `-E 'prefixDirectory="/usr/"'` to the command line is a good way to direct hyperlinks created by [installPackage](../../Core/function/installPackage.md) to the documentation provided by an older copy of Macaulay2 installed with the prefix `/usr/`, and that, in turn, is easily done within Emacs by the keystroke sequence C-u f12, which offers you a chance to edit the command line. The initial value of [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) described above can be overridden by the user's `initialization_spc_file`). The list [prefixPath](../../Core/object/prefixPath.md) should be distinguished from the list [path](../../Core/object/path.md), which is used to locate files to be loaded, by functions such as [searchPath](../../Core/function/searchPath.md), [load](../../Core/function/load.md), [loadPackage](../../Core/function/loadPackage.md), and [needsPackage](../../Core/function/needsPackage.md). The following example shows the list of places where we might find the source code of a package called `Foo` after it has been installed by [installPackage](../../Core/function/installPackage.md). This example shows the list of places where we might reasonably find the html file documenting a function named `bar` in a package called `Foo`. This example shows the list of places where we might reasonably find the info file documenting a package called `Foo`.


## Examples

```macaulay2
stack apply(prefixPath, p -> p | Layout#1#"packages" | "Foo.m2")
```
```
o1 = /home/m2user/.Macaulay2/local/share/Macaulay2/Foo.m2
/usr/share/Macaulay2/Foo.
------------------------------------------------------------------------
m2
```
```macaulay2
stack apply(prefixPath, p -> p | replace("PKG","Foo",Layout#1#"packagehtml") | "bar.html")
```
```
o2 = /home/m2user/.Macaulay2/local/share/doc/
/home/flux/.cache/yay/macaulay2/src/M2/M2/usr
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Macaulay2/Foo/html/bar.html
-dist/share/doc/Macaulay2/Foo/html/bar.html
```
```macaulay2
stack apply(prefixPath, p -> p | Layout#1#"info" | "Foo.info")
```
```
o3 = /home/m2user/.Macaulay2/local/share/info/Foo.info
/usr/share/info/Foo.info
```

# `programPaths`

User-defined external program paths

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** MutableHashTable  
**Aliases:** `Core$programPaths`  
**Properties:** mutable  

## Description

A mutable hash table containing user-defined paths to external programs used by Macaulay2.  Its keys are strings containing the names of programs and must coincide with the first argument of [findProgram](../../Core/function/findProgram.md). It is only necessary to define a path in this way if a program is installed in a non-standard location.  In particular, [findProgram](../../Core/function/findProgram.md) already checks `prefixDirectory | currentLayout#"programs"`, (where the programs shipped with Macaulay2 are installed) and all of the directories in the user's `PATH` environment variable. If you use a particular program frequently and it is installed in a non-standard location, then it may be useful to add a line to your `initialization_spc_file` defining its path in this way.

name: RevLex
markdown:
# `RevLex`

Reverse lexicographic ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$RevLex`  

## Description

The reverse lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if the FIRST non-zero entry of the vector of integers `A-B` is NEGATIVE. This is a local order, not a global order.  Therefore Gröbner bases over this ring only give generators over the local ring whose fractions are all elements not in the ideal generated by the variables. Computations of Gröbner bases for local orders are done using Mora's algorithm.


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder => RevLex, Global => false];
```
```macaulay2
a^3 + b^2 + b*c + a*c^2 + b^2*c + a + b + c
2    2           2    3
```
```
o2 = c + b + b*c + b  + b c + a + a*c  + a
o2 : R
```
## See also

- [Global](../../Core/object/Global.md)
- [GRevLex](../../Core/object/GRevLex.md)

name: to
markdown:
# `to`

For loops

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$to`  

## Description

ExamplesThe expressions in this construction may be arbitrarily complicated. Here is an example where `z` is a sequence of expressions separated by semicolons (see [;](../../Core/operator/_scol_.md)). The `do z` clause may be omitted. The `from m` clause may be omitted, in which case `i` starts with `0`. The `when p` clause may be omitted. The `to n` clause may be omitted. The `list x` clause may be omitted. If [continue](../../Core/object/continue.md) is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, no value is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `continue w` is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, the value of `w` is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `break v` is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and `v` is returned as its value. If [break](../../Core/object/break.md) is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and the list accumulated so far is returned as the value. If `v` is an instance of any class with the [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) method installed (e.g., a string), then the values of `i` are obtained by repeatedly calling [next](../../Core/function/next.md) on the output of `iterator v` until [StopIteration](../../Core/object/StopIteration.md) is returned.### CaveatThe variable `i` is a new local variable whose scope includes only the expressions `p`, `x`, and `z` in the body of the loop.  Moreover, new local variables defined inside the body of the loop will not be visible outside it.

markdown:
# `try`

Catch an error

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$try`  

## Description

The return value is the value returned by y or z, as the case may be. The clause `then y` may be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by x if there is no error or alarm. The clause `else z` may be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by y, unless an error or alarm occurs, in which case [null](../../Core/object/null.md) is returned. The clauses `then y else z` may both be omitted, in which case the return value is the value returned by x, unless an error or alarm occurs, in which case [null](../../Core/object/null.md) is returned. In the alternate form `try x then y except err do z`, x is first evaluated. If no error occurs, then the value of y is returned, or the value of x if the `then y` clause is omitted. If an error occurs, then the corresponding [Error](../../Core/type/Error.md) object is assigned to the symbol specified by err. That symbol is then available during the evaluation of z, whose value is returned. The behavior of interrupts (other than alarms) is unaffected.### CaveatWe will change the behavior of this function soon so that it will be possible to catch errors of a particular type.  Meanwhile, users are recommended to use this function sparingly, if at all.

markdown:
# `TypicalValue`

Make a new method function

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$TypicalValue`  

## Description

The code above creates a method function that takes up to four arguments, looking up the appropriate method according to the classes of the arguments, with inheritance.  To install a method for two arguments, (x, y), of classes X and Y, use code like this:     f(X, Y) := (x, y) -> ...where '...' represents the body of the function you wish to install. The syntax for one or three arguments is analogous.  See [:=](../../Core/operator/_col__eq_.md) for details. In the following example we install a asymmetric method to illustrate the left-associative order of evaluation for a binary method function. By default, at most four arguments (in a sequence) can be handled by a method function, and the types have to be considered separately when installing methods. In this example, we define a method function that treats a sequence as a single argument, and we install a method for handling such arguments. Here we define a method whose first argument is to be a type.  It will convert its second argument to that type. In the next example we make a linear function of a single real variable whose coefficients are provided as optional arguments named Slope and Intercept, with default value 1. The methods installed for this method function should be written in the form `opts -> args -> (...)`.  The argument `opts` will be assigned a hash table of type [OptionTable](../../Core/type/OptionTable.md) containing the optional argument names and their current values.  For example, in the body of the function, the current value for the argument named `b` can be recovered with `opts#b`, or with `opts.b`, in case `b` is known to be a global symbol.  Be careful not to change the value of `b`, or the code will stop working; it would be a good idea to protect it. The default [OptionTable](../../Core/type/OptionTable.md) for `r` can be recovered with the function [options](../../Core/function/options.md).  The options given to [method](../../Core/function/method.md) can be recovered with [methodOptions](../../Core/function/methodOptions.md). In the next example we define a method function that leaves option processing to the individual methods. For now, one installs a method function for `s` with no non-optional arguments using [installMethod](../../Core/function/installMethod.md):### Functions with optional argument named TypicalValue: For the programmerThe object [TypicalValue](../../Core/object/TypicalValue.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).

name: Up
markdown:
# `Up`

Monomial ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Up`  

## Description

`MonomialOrder` -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic). In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations. In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of ordering tests, of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see `monomial_spc_orderings`. Permissible elements:[GRevLex](../../Core/object/GRevLex.md) => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables[Lex](../../Core/object/Lex.md) => n[Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md) => {...}[Position](../../Core/object/Position.md) => Up  or  Position => Down[RevLex](../../Core/object/RevLex.md) => n[GroupLex](../../Core/object/GroupLex.md) => n[GroupRevLex](../../Core/object/GroupRevLex.md) => n[MonomialSize](../../Core/object/MonomialSize.md) => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variablesSome examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list.`MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}` -- a product order`MonomialOrder => {2, 3}` -- same`MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}` -- a weight order`MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}` -- sameIf any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option `Global => false` should be used.


## Examples

```macaulay2
QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]
```
```
o1 = QQ[x..y]
o1 : PolynomialRing
```
```macaulay2
x<1
```
```
o2 = true
```
```macaulay2
y<1
```
```
o3 = false
```

name: Weights
markdown:
# `Weights`

Assigning weights to the variables

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$Weights`  

## Description

Given a list L of n integers, the weight order on a polynomial ring in n variables is defined by: x^A > x^B if A_1 L_1 + ... + A_n L_n > B_1 L_1 + ... + B_n L_n. The leading component of a polynomial under a weight order need not be a monomial.  When two monomials have the same weight, by default they are further distinguished with the GRevLex order. However, we can retrieve the entire leading component with the command `leadTerm(1, f)`. The plain `leadTerm f` is in this case the same as `leadTerm(2, f)`: they both use the full specification of the monomial ordering, first by weight and then by the `GRevLex` order.  In contrast, `leadTerm(1, f)`only distinguishes monomials by the first, i.e., weight, specification. The weight order may be combined with further ordering elements to break ties. In the following example, we use a second weight vector to break ties under first weight vector.`leadTerm(3, ideal(f))` uses both the specified weights and the `GRevLex` order to calculate the leading component. When the number of weights is smaller than the number of variables, the remaining variables are given weight 0. In the following example, `c` and `d` have weight 0.### Functions with optional argument named Weights: For the programmerThe object [Weights](../../Core/object/Weights.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {-1,2,3,4}},Global=>false];
```
```macaulay2
f = a^2 + b+ c^2 + b*d
2              2
```
```
o2 = c  + b*d + b + a
o2 : R
```
```macaulay2
leadTerm f
2
```

```
o3 = c
o3 : R
```
```macaulay2
leadTerm(1,ideal(f))
2
```
```
o4 = ideal(c  + b*d)
o4 : Ideal of R
```
```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2,3,4}, Weights => {2,4,2,1}}];
```
```macaulay2
f = a^6 + b^3+ c^2
6    3    2
```
```
o6 = a  + b  + c
o6 : R
```
```macaulay2
leadTerm(f)
6
```
```
o7 = a
o7 : R
```
```macaulay2
leadTerm(1, ideal(f))
6    3    2
```
```
o8 = ideal(a  + b  + c )
o8 : Ideal of R
```
```macaulay2

```
```

o9 : Ideal of R
```


name: WeylAlgebra
markdown:
# `WeylAlgebra`

Specify differential operators in the ring

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Symbol  
**Aliases:** `Core$WeylAlgebra`  

## Description

The `WeylAlgebra` option may be used to provide a list of variables and their corresponding differential operators in a Weyl algebra. For instance, an option of the form `x => dx` specifies that `dx` plays the role of the derivative with respect to `x` in the resulting Weyl algebra. Note that only when the monoid is used to create a polynomial ring the Weyl algebra variables take effect. There are multiple acceptable ways to populate this option, but the differential variable always has to come to the right of the corresponding algebra variable. The package `Dmodules` contains further methods for creating and manipulating Weyl algebras. Lastly, if a single variable is provided at the end, it is used as a homogenizing variable. This option may also be used when creating a new ring from an existing ring, creating a tensor product ring, or symmetric algebra.### Functions with optional argument named WeylAlgebra: For the programmerThe object [WeylAlgebra](../../Core/object/WeylAlgebra.md) is a [Symbol](../../Core/type/Symbol.md).

name: when
markdown:
# `when`

For loops

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Keyword  
**Aliases:** `Core$when`  

## Description

ExamplesThe expressions in this construction may be arbitrarily complicated. Here is an example where `z` is a sequence of expressions separated by semicolons (see [;](../../Core/operator/_scol_.md)). The `do z` clause may be omitted. The `from m` clause may be omitted, in which case `i` starts with `0`. The `when p` clause may be omitted. The `to n` clause may be omitted. The `list x` clause may be omitted. If [continue](../../Core/object/continue.md) is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, no value is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `continue w` is executed by `x` then execution of `x` is interrupted, the value of `w` is added to the list, and iteration of the loop continues. If `break v` is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and `v` is returned as its value. If [break](../../Core/object/break.md) is executed by `x`, then the loop is stopped and the list accumulated so far is returned as the value. If `v` is an instance of any class with the [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) method installed (e.g., a string), then the values of `i` are obtained by repeatedly calling [next](../../Core/function/next.md) on the output of `iterator v` until [StopIteration](../../Core/object/StopIteration.md) is returned.### CaveatThe variable `i` is a new local variable whose scope includes only the expressions `p`, `x`, and `z` in the body of the loop.  Moreover, new local variables defined inside the body of the loop will not be visible outside it.


## Examples

name: BettiTally
markdown:
# `BettiTally`

The class of all Betti tallies

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$BettiTally`  

## Description

A Betti tally is a special type of [Tally](../../Core/type/Tally.md) that is printed as a display of graded Betti numbers. The class was created so the function [betti](../../Core/function/betti.md) could return something that both prints nicely and from which information can be extracted.  The keys are triples `(i, d, h)` encoding:`i`, the column labels, representing the homological degree; `d`, a list of integers giving a multidegree; and `h`, the row labels, representing the dot product of a weight covector and `d`. Only `i` and `h` are used in printing, and the weight covector can be modified by specifying the `betti_lpar__dot__dot__dot__cma_Weights_eq__gt__dot__dot__dot__rpar_` option to `betti_lpar_BettiTally_rpar_`. For convenience, the operations of direct sum ([++](../../Core/operator/_add__add_.md)), tensor product ([**](../../Core/operator/_mul__mul_.md)), [codim](../../Core/function/codim.md), [degree](../../Core/function/degree.md), [dual](../../Core/function/dual.md), [pdim](../../Core/function/pdim.md), [poincare](../../Core/function/poincare.md), [regularity](../../Core/function/regularity.md), and degree shifting (numbers in brackets or parentheses), have been implemented for Betti tallies.  These operations mimic the corresponding operations on chain complexes. If the Betti tally represents the Betti numbers of a resolution of a module $M$ on a polynomial ring $R = K[x_0,..., x_n]$, then while the data does not uniquely determine $M$, it suffices to compute the [hilbertPolynomial](../../Core/function/hilbertPolynomial.md) and [hilbertSeries](../../Core/function/hilbertSeries.md) of $M$. A Betti tally can be multiplied by an integer or by a rational number, and the values can be lifted to integers, when possible.### Types of Betti tally: Types of Betti tally:[MultigradedBettiTally](../../Core/type/MultigradedBettiTally.md)Functions and methods returning a Betti tally:[betti](../../Core/function/betti.md)BettiTally ** BettiTallyBettiTally ++ BettiTallyBettiTally ArrayBettiTally ZZdual(BettiTally)lift(BettiTally, type of ZZ)QQ * BettiTallyZZ * BettiTally[minimalBetti](../../Core/function/minimalBetti.md)minimalBetti(Ideal) -- see [minimalBetti](../../Core/function/minimalBetti.md)minimalBetti(Module) -- see [minimalBetti](../../Core/function/minimalBetti.md)`truncate_lpar_BettiTally_cma_InfiniteNumber_cma_InfiniteNumber_rpar_``truncate_lpar_BettiTally_cma_InfiniteNumber_cma_ZZ_rpar_``truncate_lpar_BettiTally_cma_ZZ_cma_InfiniteNumber_rpar_``truncate_lpar_BettiTally_cma_ZZ_cma_ZZ_rpar_`Methods that use a Betti tally:`betti_lpar_BettiTally_rpar_`codim(BettiTally)degree(BettiTally)hilbertPolynomial(ZZ, BettiTally)hilbertSeries(ZZ, BettiTally)pdim(BettiTally)poincare(BettiTally)regularity(BettiTally)multigraded(BettiTally) -- see [multigraded](../../Core/function/multigraded.md)`Ring_spc__pow__spc_BettiTally`For the programmerThe object [BettiTally](../../Core/type/BettiTally.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [VirtualTally](../../Core/type/VirtualTally.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `CacheTable`

Hash tables for caching

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$CacheTable`  

## Description

A cache table is a type of mutable hash table designed for caching computed values that may be recalled later. Cache tables are designed so their contents will not participate in any comparisons by the strict comparison operator `===`. To that end, any two cache tables with the same class and parent are considered equal to each other and have hash code equal to 0.


## Examples

```macaulay2
A = { 1, 2, new CacheTable from { 1 => 10,  2 => 20 }}
```
```
o1 = {1, 2, CacheTable{...2...}}
o1 : List
```
```macaulay2
B = { 1, 2, new CacheTable from { 1 => 100, 2 => 200 }}
```
```
o2 = {1, 2, CacheTable{...2...}}
o2 : List
```
```macaulay2
A === B
```
```
o3 = true
```
```macaulay2
hash A#2
```
```
o4 = 0
```
```macaulay2
hash B#2
```
```
o5 = 0
```
**Parent:** `MutableHashTable`

## Ancestors

`MutableHashTable` > `HashTable` > `Thing`

# `CC`

The class of all complex numbers

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** InexactFieldFamily  
**Aliases:** `ℂ`, `Core$ℂ`, `Core$CC`  

## Description

In Macaulay2, complex numbers are represented as floating point numbers, and so are only approximate.  The symbol [ii](../../Core/object/ii.md) represents the square root of -1 in many numeric contexts.  A complex number is obtained by using the symbolic constant [ii](../../Core/object/ii.md) or the conversion functions [toCC](../../Core/function/toCC.md) and [numeric](../../Core/function/numeric.md), in combination with real numbers (see [RR](../../Core/type/RR.md)). It is stored internally as a pair of arbitrary precision floating point real numbers, using the `MPFR` library. Complex numbers are ordered lexicographically, mingled with real numbers. The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using [precision](../../Core/function/precision.md). For complex numbers, the functions [class](../../Core/function/class.md) and [ring](../../Core/function/ring.md) yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision. A computation involving numbers of different precisions has a result with the minimal precision occurring. Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.)Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by [printingPrecision](../../Core/object/printingPrecision.md). Use [toExternalString](../../Core/function/toExternalString.md) to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before.### CaveatCurrently, most # `CCi`

The class of all complex intervals

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** InexactFieldFamily  
**Aliases:** `Core$CCi`  

## Description

A complex interval is entered as a pair of real intervals to the [interval](../../Core/function/interval.md) function.  It is stored internally as a pair of arbitrary precision intervals using the `MPFI` library. The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using [precision](../../Core/function/precision.md). Complex intervals are objects in [class](../../Core/function/class.md) CCi which is an [InexactFieldFamily](../../Core/type/InexactFieldFamily.md). For complex intervals, the functions [class](../../Core/function/class.md) and [ring](../../Core/function/ring.md) yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision. The precision can be specified on input by specifying the precision of both input [CC](../../Core/type/CC.md) numbers. Alternatively, the precision can be specified by including the option `Precision`. Complex intervals can also be created using `span_lpar_Sequence_rpar_` to create the smallest complex axis-aligned rectangle containing the inputs. Operations using complex intervals are computed as sets so that the resulting intervals contain all possible outputs from pairs of points in input intervals. The real and imaginary parts of a complex interval can be accessed with [realPart](../../Core/function/realPart.md) and [imaginaryPart](../../Core/function/imaginaryPart.md).  These are real intervals of class [RRi](../../Core/type/RRi.md). # `Command`

The class of all commands

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** SelfInitializingType

## Description

A command behaves as a function does if it is followed by an adjacent expression that can serve as its argument or argument list. name: Eliminate
markdown:
# `Eliminate`

Elimination order

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** SelfInitializingType  
**Aliases:** `Core$Eliminate`  

## Description

The option `Eliminate => n` is a shortcut for `Weights => {n:1}` The remaining variables are given weight 0. The monomial order is the elimination order eliminating the first n variables, refined by the graded reverse lexicographic order. This order enables intersections with the subring consisting of all but the first 3 variables. For this, use the command [selectInSubring](../../Core/function/selectInSubring.md). Eliminate may be combined with block orders as well. In the last example, the order is block order: the first four variables are in the first block, the subsequent two variables are in the second block, the remaining variables are in the third block, and the weights of the variables are 1,1,1,0,..., 0. We illustrate the usage of [selectInSubring](../../Core/function/selectInSubring.md).### CaveatIf the number of degree vectors is greater than one, this is currently only graded using the first degree vector.  This will eventually change.


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..i, MonomialOrder => Eliminate 3];
```
```macaulay2
I = ideal(a^2, b-f, d^4, i - b);
```
```
o2 : Ideal of R
```
```macaulay2
selectInSubring(1, gens gb I)
```
```
o3 = | f-i d4 |
1      2
o3 : Matrix R  <-- R
```
```macaulay2
R = QQ[a..i, MonomialOrder => {Eliminate 3,4,2}];
```
```macaulay2
d^3 - a*e^4 + b^2*i + a*c*d*f +a*c^2*g + a*c*g
2               2               4    3
```
```
o5 = a*c g + a*c*d*f + b i + a*c*g - a*e  + d
o5 : R
```
```macaulay2
I = ideal(a..i)
```
```
o6 = ideal (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i)
o6 : Ideal of R
```
```macaulay2
selectInSubring(1, gens gb I);
1      6
```
```
o7 : Matrix R  <-- R
```
```macaulay2
selectInSubring(2, gens gb I);
1      5
```
```
o8 : Matrix R  <-- R
```
```macaulay2
selectInSubring(3, gens gb I);
1      3
```
```
o9 : Matrix R  <-- R
```

name: Expression

# `Expression`

The class of all expressions

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Expression`  

## Description

An expression is a symbolic representation of a mathematical expression.  It retains some of the semantics of the mathematical expression, as well as enough information to print the expression nicely.  In Macaulay2 expressions have two main functions: they are an intermediate phase in the conversion of a mathematical object to a [net](../../Core/function/net.md) that can be printed; and they are a way of holding and displaying a mathematical expression in an unevaluated form that can be both printed and evaluated. Internally, each expression is a basic list whose elements may also be expressions.  The elements that are not expressions are interpreted as themselves, and may be strings, symbols, numbers, etc.  There are several types of expression that correspond to various sorts of mathematical entities, such as sums of class [Sum](../../Core/type/Sum.md), products, of class [Product](../../Core/type/Product.md), fractions of class [Divide](../../Core/type/Divide.md), etc. Expressions are produced with the function [expression](../../Core/function/expression.md).  The various methods installed for it try to bring as much of the semantic structure of the mathematical object to light.  The following examples illustrate that, using [peek](../../Core/function/peek.md) and [peek'](../../Core/function/peek_1qt_.md) to display the internal structure. The function [factor](../../Core/function/factor.md) returns an expression. Expressions can be evaluated using [value](../../Core/function/value.md). The following operators can be applied to expressions: [SPACE](../../Core/operator/SPACE.md), [*](../../Core/operator/_mul_.md), [**](../../Core/operator/_mul__mul_.md), [+](../../Core/operator/_add_.md), [-](../../Core/operator/-.md), [/](../../Core/operator/_slash_.md), [==](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq_.md), [^](../../Core/operator/_pow_.md), and [_](../../Core/operator/_us_.md).  They are contagious, in the sense that when applied to an expression and a non-expression, the non-expression will be converted to an expression and the operator will be applied.  Only the most trivial algebraic simplifications are applied.### Types of expression: Types of expression:[Adjacent](../../Core/type/Adjacent.md)[AssociativeExpression](../../Core/type/AssociativeExpression.md)[BinaryOperation](../../Core/type/BinaryOperation.md)[Divide](../../Core/type/Divide.md)[FunctionApplication](../../Core/type/FunctionApplication.md)[Holder](../../Core/type/Holder.md)[MapExpression](../../Core/type/MapExpression.md)[MatrixExpression](../../Core/type/MatrixExpression.md)[Minus](../../Core/type/Minus.md)[Power](../../Core/type/Power.md)[RowExpression](../../Core/type/RowExpression.md)[SparseMonomialVectorExpression](../../Core/type/SparseMonomialVectorExpression.md)[SparseVectorExpression](../../Core/type/SparseVectorExpression.md)[Subscript](../../Core/type/Subscript.md)[Superscript](../../Core/type/Superscript.md)[Table](../../Core/type/Table.md)[VectorExpression](../../Core/type/VectorExpression.md)Functions and methods returning an expression:[expression](../../Core/function/expression.md)`expression_lpar_SheafMap_rpar_`[hold](../../Core/function/hold.md)Methods that use an expression: assert(Expression) -- see [assert](../../Core/function/assert.md)`value_lpar_Expression_rpar_`For the programmerThe object [Expression](../../Core/type/Expression.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `FractionField`

The class of all fraction fields

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$FractionField`  

## Description

Macaulay2 provides for fraction fields of integral domains. In some cases, normal forms of fractions makes sense, but in general for fraction fields of quotient rings, there is no notion of normal form for a fraction. In other words, fractions may be equal without displaying the same numerator and denominator. Computations over fraction fields, or polynomial rings over fraction fields, especially Gröbner basis computations, are much slower than over prime fields. Still, an attempt is made to speed up these computations as much as possible, and more is planned in the future. For an overview, see `fraction_spc_fields` and  [frac](../../Core/function/frac.md). Useful functions for use with fractions and fraction fields include:[frac](../../Core/function/frac.md)[numerator](../../Core/function/numerator.md)[denominator](../../Core/function/denominator.md)[liftable](../../Core/function/liftable.md)[lift](../../Core/function/lift.md)### Functions and methods returning a fraction field: Functions and methods returning a fraction field:[frac](../../Core/function/frac.md)Methods that use a fraction field: degrees(FractionField) -- see `degrees_lpar_Ring_rpar_`describe(FractionField) -- see [describe](../../Core/function/describe.md)dim(FractionField) -- see `dim_lpar_Ring_rpar_`frac(FractionField) -- see [frac](../../Core/function/frac.md)numgens(FractionField) -- see `numgens_lpar_Ring_rpar_`precision(FractionField) -- see [precision](../../Core/function/precision.md)For the programmerThe object [FractionField](../../Core/type/FractionField.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [EngineRing](../../Core/type/EngineRing.md) < [Ring](../../Core/type/Ring.md) < [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md) < [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

The class of all hash tables

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type

## Description

A hash table consists of: a class type, a parent type, and a set of key-value pairs.  The keys and values can be anything. The access functions below accept a key and return the corresponding value.  For details of the mechanism underlying this, see `hashing`. One important feature of hash tables that when the keys are consecutive integers starting at 0, the keys are scanned in the natural order. There is a subclass of HashTable called [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md) which consists of those hash tables whose entries can be changed. # `HeaderType`

A class of lists with abbreviated constructors

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$HeaderType`  

## Description

These are the types `X` of lists that can be constructed by expressions of the form `X {a, b, c,...}`.  They also act on sequences.### Methods that use a header type: Methods that use a header type: HeaderType ListHeaderType SequenceProtected objects of class `HeaderType`:[Adjacent](../../Core/type/Adjacent.md)[BinaryOperation](../../Core/type/BinaryOperation.md)[Divide](../../Core/type/Divide.md)[Equation](../../Core/type/Equation.md)[FunctionApplication](../../Core/type/FunctionApplication.md)[MapExpression](../../Core/type/MapExpression.md)[MatrixExpression](../../Core/type/MatrixExpression.md)[Power](../../Core/type/Power.md)[RowExpression](../../Core/type/RowExpression.md)[SparseMonomialVectorExpression](../../Core/type/SparseMonomialVectorExpression.md)[SparseVectorExpression](../../Core/type/SparseVectorExpression.md)[Subscript](../../Core/type/Subscript.md)[Superscript](../../Core/type/Superscript.md)[Table](../../Core/type/Table.md)[VectorExpression](../../Core/type/VectorExpression.md)For the programmerThe object [HeaderType](../../Core/type/HeaderType.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md) < [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).


## Examples

```macaulay2
X = new HeaderType of BasicList
```

name: Holder

# `Holder`

The class of all holder expressions

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** WrapperType  
**Aliases:** `Core$Holder`  

## Description

This type of expression is a container for a single, arbitrary, thing that is basic enough that the correct method for printing does not depend on its neighbors in the containing expression.  A negative number would not be basic enough for this purpose, since as a member of a sum, it would require special treatment.### Types of holder: Types of holder:[Describe](../../Core/type/Describe.md)[OneExpression](../../Core/type/OneExpression.md)[Parenthesize](../../Core/type/Parenthesize.md)[ZeroExpression](../../Core/type/ZeroExpression.md)For the programmerThe object [Holder](../../Core/type/Holder.md) is a [WrapperType](../../Core/type/WrapperType.md), with ancestor classes [Expression](../../Core/type/Expression.md) < [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `ImmutableType`

The class of all immutable types

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$ImmutableType`  

## Description

All types are implemented as hash tables.  Most types are mutable, so that additional methods for handling their instances can be added at any time.  However, if a type has an ancestor where the methods can be stored, then mutability is not needed. When a type is used to represent a mathematical object, then immutability is desirable, in order to make the strict equality operator work on it.  For example, a module `M` is a type, with its elements are its instances, but we would like to be able to compare two modules quickly, and form sets of modules.  This is possible, because we have implemented modules as immutable types, and we have put the methods for adding and subtracting elements of `M` into the class [Vector](../../Core/type/Vector.md). Another advantage of immutability of modules is that there is no particular reason, aside from efficiency, to avoid creating a given module multiple times, as one copy of the module is as good as another.### Types of immutable type: Types of immutable type:[Module](../../Core/type/Module.md)Methods that use an immutable type: ofClass(ImmutableType) -- see [ofClass](../../Core/function/ofClass.md)For the programmerThe object [ImmutableType](../../Core/type/ImmutableType.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `IndexedVariable`

The class of all indexed variables

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$IndexedVariable`  

## Description

Indexed variables provide the possibility of producing polynomial rings `R[x_0, x_1, ..., x_(n-1)]` in n variables, where n is not known in advance.  If `x` is an symbol, and i is an integer, then `x_i` produces an indexed variable. After this has been done, an assignment `x_i=v` will assign another value to it.  A new sequence of indexed variables of length n assigned to the symbol `x` can be produced with `x_1 .. x_n` and that sequence can be used in constructing a polynomial ring. Warning: the values of the indexed variables `t_i` are stored in a global location, behind the scenes, so may not get garbage collected, even if `t` is a local variable.### Methods that use an indexed variable: Methods that use an indexed variable: IndexedVariable <- Thing -- see [<-](../../Core/operator/_lt_-.md)IndexedVariable ? # `InexactFieldFamily`

The class of all families of inexact fields

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$InexactFieldFamily`  

## Description

All real numbers have the same class, [RR](../../Core/type/RR.md), but the rings they belong to depends on the number of binary digits of precision used to represent them.  Similarly for complex numbers, which all belong to the class [CC](../../Core/type/CC.md).  Thus [RR](../../Core/type/RR.md) and [CC](../../Core/type/CC.md) are regarded not as inexact fields, but as families of inexact fields.### Methods that use an inexact field family: Methods that use an inexact field family: default(InexactFieldFamily) -- see [default](../../Core/function/default.md)InexactFieldFamily Array -- see `Ring_spc_Array`InexactFieldFamily List -- see `Ring_spc_List`InexactFieldFamily Monoid -- see `Ring_spc_Monoid`Protected objects of class `InexactFieldFamily`:[CC](../../Core/type/CC.md)[CCi](../../Core/type/CCi.md)[RR](../../Core/type/RR.md)[RRi](../../Core/type/RRi.md)For the programmerThe object [InexactFieldFamily](../../Core/type/InexactFieldFamily.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [RingFamily](../../Core/type/RingFamily.md) < [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md) < [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `Iterator`

Class for iterators

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** SelfInitializingType  
**Aliases:** `Core$Iterator`  

## Description

This is a class designed to simplify writing [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) methods. Each instance is a nullary [FunctionClosure](../../Core/type/FunctionClosure.md) that serves as the [next](../../Core/function/next.md) method for the iterator. Each call of `next iter` is equivalent to `iter()`. Every `Iterator` object is an iterator for itself. However, we cannot "rewind" an `Iterator` object.  Every time that it is iterated upon using [for](../../Core/object/for.md), [scan](../../Core/function/scan.md), etc., iteration will resume where it left off previously. Contrast this with most other classes with the [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md) method installed, like, strings, for which a new `Iterator` object is created every time it is iterated upon, and so iteration starts over from the beginning### Functions and methods returning an iterator: Functions and methods returning an iterator: accumulate(Function, Thing) -- see [accumulate](../../Core/function/accumulate.md)accumulate(Function, Thing, Thing) -- see [accumulate](../../Core/function/accumulate.md)`apply_lpar_Thing_cma_Function_rpar_`applyPairs(Thing, Function) -- see [applyPairs](../../Core/function/applyPairs.md)`select_lpar_Thing_cma_Function_rpar_`Methods that use an iterator: iterator(Iterator) -- see [iterator](../../Core/function/iterator.md)`Iterator_spc__pipe__spc_Iterator`next(Iterator) -- see [next](../../Core/function/next.md)For the programmerThe object [Iterator](../../Core/type/Iterator.md) is a [SelfInitializingType](../../Core/type/SelfInitializingType.md), with ancestor classes [FunctionClosure](../../Core/type/FunctionClosure.md) < [Function](../../Core/type/Function.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `List`

The class of all lists -- {...}

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$List`  

## Description

Lists in Macaulay2 consist of elements of any type, enclosed in braces, and separated by commas. The length of a list has two notations, the version with the `#` is faster when writing programs. The first entry of the list has index 0.  Indexing is performed using [#](../../Core/operator/_hash_.md). Lists in Macaulay2 are immutable. See [MutableList](../../Core/type/MutableList.md) for making and using lists that you may modify. To convert lists to and from other types of [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md), in addition to [toList](../../Core/function/toList.md), one may use [new](../../Core/object/new.md).
