# `LocalDictionary`

The class of all local dictionaries

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$LocalDictionary`  

## Description

A local dictionary is one used in connection with a local scope, such as one that is bounded by the body of a function closure. A local dictionary is created on the fly by the interpreter, and after the scope has been closed, the dictionary can be enlarged no further. Accessing local dictionaries can be a useful debugging tool.  The local dictionaries accessible to the user come with frames, so their symbols have values; thus they may be referred to as dictionary closures.### Methods that use an object of class LocalDictionary: Methods that use an object of class LocalDictionary:`debug_lpar_LocalDictionary_rpar_`For the programmerThe object [LocalDictionary](../../Core/type/LocalDictionary.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [Dictionary](../../Core/type/Dictionary.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `Matrix`

The class of all matrices

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Matrix`  

## Description

A matrix is a homomorphism between two modules, together with an integer (or vector of integers) called its degree, which is used when determining whether the map is homogeneous.  The matrix is stored in the usual way as a rectangular array of ring elements. When the source or target modules are not free, the matrix is interpreted as a linear transformation in terms of the generators of the modules. A matrix `f` is an immutable object, so if you want to cache information about it, put it in the hash table `f.cache`. # `MatrixExpression`

The class of all matrix expressions

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** HeaderType  
**Aliases:** `Core$MatrixExpression`  

## Description

`MatrixExpression` is a type of [Expression](../../Core/type/Expression.md) representing a matrix.


## Examples

```macaulay2
MatrixExpression {{a,b,c},{a,bb,ccc}}
```
```
o1 = | a b  c   |
| a bb ccc |
o1 : Expression of class MatrixExpression
```
```macaulay2
R=QQ[x,y];
```
```macaulay2
MatrixExpression append(applyTable({{x^2-y^2,x^3-y^3},{x^2-4*y^2,x^3+y^3}},factor),Degrees=>{{{-2},{-3}},{{0},{0}}})
```
```
o3 = {-2} | (x-y)(x+y)   (x-y)(x2+xy+y2) |
{-3} | (x-2y)(x+2y) (x+y)(x2-xy+y2) |
o3 : Expression of class MatrixExpression
```
```macaulay2
value oo
```
```
o4 = {-2} | x2-y2  x3-y3 |
{-3} | x2-4y2 x3+y3 |
2      2
o4 : Matrix R  <-- R
```
**Parent:** `Expression`

A multigraded Betti tally is a special type of [BettiTally](../../Core/type/BettiTally.md) that is printed as a diagram of the multigraded Betti numbers. The class was created so that the method `multigraded_lpar_BettiTally_rpar_` could return something that both prints nicely and from which information could be extracted. The content of a multigraded Betti tally is identical to the Betti tally from which it was constructed. By default the data is presented as a table of polynomials where each column corresponds to a given homological degree appearing as the top entry and each monomial in the other entries represents the multidegree of a given summand. When [compactMatrixForm](../../Core/object/compactMatrixForm.md) is set to `false`, the entries represent the multidegree of summands ordered by the total weight. The number of summands corresponding to a given multidegree appears to the left of the multidegree. For convenience, various operations on `BettiTally` such as direct sum ([++](../../Core/operator/_add__add_.md)), tensor product ([**](../../Core/operator/_mul__mul_.md)), [pdim](../../Core/function/pdim.md) and degree shifting (numbers in brackets or parentheses) are extended to work with multigraded Betti tables. These operations mimic the corresponding operations on chain complexes.### ContributorsThis feature was implemented by Mahrud Sayrafi based on earlier work by Gregory G. Smith.### Functions and methods returning a multigraded Betti tally: Functions and methods returning a multigraded Betti tally: multigraded(BettiTally) -- see [multigraded](../../Core/function/multigraded.md)Methods that use a multigraded Betti tally: MultigradedBettiTally Sequence`MultigradedBettiTally_spc_List`For the programmerThe object [MultigradedBettiTally](../../Core/type/MultigradedBettiTally.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [BettiTally](../../Core/type/BettiTally.md) < [VirtualTally](../../Core/type/VirtualTally.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `MutableList`

The class of all mutable lists

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$MutableList`  

## Description

For an overview of lists and sequences, see `lists_spc_and_spc_sequences`. Normally the entries in a mutable list are not printed, to prevent infinite loops in the printing routines.  To print them out, use [peek](../../Core/function/peek.md). To construct a mutable list with a given length and whose entries are all [null](../../Core/object/null.md), provide an integer. If a value is assigned at a position that is not yet present in a mutable list, then it grows accordingly, and any intermediate positions are filled with [null](../../Core/object/null.md). # `MutableMatrix`

The class of all mutable matrices

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$MutableMatrix`  

## Description

A mutable matrix in Macaulay2 is a rectangular array of elements of a specific ring, whose entries can be modified. A mutable matrix is different from a [Matrix](../../Core/type/Matrix.md) in that a matrix contains degree information for the target and source of the matrix, while a mutable matrix has no such information.  Also, more operations are provided for matrices. For an overview of mutable matrices, see `mutable_spc_matrices`. Mutable matrices can either be encoded in a sparse manner (the matrix only encodes the non-zero elements), or in a dense manner (all elements are stored -- even zeros).  The distinction is an option to several of the routines that create mutable matrices ([mutableMatrix](../../Core/function/mutableMatrix.md), [mutableIdentity](../../Core/function/mutableIdentity.md)). Certain operations over RR or CC are performed using the LAPACK library and require dense encoding of matrices: [LUdecomposition](../../Core/function/LUdecomposition.md), [SVD](../../Core/function/SVD.md), [solve](../../Core/function/solve.md), [eigenvalues](../../Core/function/eigenvalues.md), [eigenvectors](../../Core/function/eigenvectors.md).row and column operations[rowAdd](../../Core/function/rowAdd.md)[rowSwap](../../Core/function/rowSwap.md)[rowPermute](../../Core/function/rowPermute.md)[rowMult](../../Core/function/rowMult.md)[columnAdd](../../Core/function/columnAdd.md)[columnSwap](../../Core/function/columnSwap.md)[columnPermute](../../Core/function/columnPermute.md)[columnMult](../../Core/function/columnMult.md)matrix arithmeticMany matrix arithmetic routines are only available for immutable matrices, not mutable matrices. # `Mutex`

The class of mutexes

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Mutex`  

## Description

A mutex (short for mutual exclusion) is a synchronization primitive used to prevent multiple threads from accessing shared data at the same time. It ensures that only one thread can hold the lock at a time, which helps avoid race conditions in concurrent programs. In Macaulay2, a `Mutex` object can be used to protect critical sections of code. When a thread locks a mutex, other threads attempting to lock it will wait until it is unlocked. For example, suppose multiple threads try to modify the same string. Each thread will need to get the current value of the string, make its modification, and then save the new value.  However, there is a good chance that another thread might save its updated value after another thread has fetched it but before it saved the new value.  We can see this in the code below. We likely ended up with fewer than the expected number of 10 messages. We can get around this issue by using a mutex to lock the string so that only one thread can modify it at a time. With the mutex, all 10 messages are present.### Methods that use a mutex: Methods that use a mutex: lock(Mutex) -- see [lock](../../Core/function/lock.md)`new_spc_Mutex`tryLock(Mutex) -- see [tryLock](../../Core/function/tryLock.md)unlock(Mutex) -- see [unlock](../../Core/function/unlock.md)For the programmerThe object [Mutex](../../Core/type/Mutex.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor class [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `Net`

The class of all nets and strings

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Net`  

## Description

A net is a generalization of a string that is designed to facilitate two-dimensional printing on ascii terminals.  It consists of a rectangular array of characters subdivided horizontally by an imaginary baseline. Operations on nets also accept strings by interpreting a string as a rectangle of height one with the baseline just below it.  In fact, the parent of [String](../../Core/type/String.md) is [Net](../../Core/type/Net.md). Multiple nets per line can be sent to an output file with [<<](../../Core/operator/_lt__lt_.md) but care must be taken to use [endl](../../Core/function/endl.md) to end lines, for nets with new line characters embedded in them will be displayed in an unexpected way. Warning: if so many characters are written to a file that an internal buffer is filled before the line ends or first net is seen, then the buffer will be flushed, and writing a net subsequently will produce an unexpected result.### Types of net: Types of net:[String](../../Core/type/String.md)Functions and methods returning a net:[generateAssertions](../../Core/function/generateAssertions.md)horizontalJoin(BasicList) -- see [horizontalJoin](../../Core/function/horizontalJoin.md)[net](../../Core/function/net.md)`Net_spc__pow__spc_ZZ`String ^ ZZ -- see `Net_spc__pow__spc_ZZ``Net_spc__pipe__spc_Net``Net_spc__pipe__pipe__spc_Net``net_lpar_Digraph_rpar_`[peek](../../Core/function/peek.md)[peek'](../../Core/function/peek_1qt_.md)stack(BasicList) -- see [stack](../../Core/function/stack.md)`String_spc__pow__spc_Sequence`Methods that use a net:# Net -- see `_hash__spc_List`capture(Net) -- see [capture](../../Core/function/capture.md)`depth_lpar_Net_rpar_``height_lpar_Net_rpar_`length(Net) -- see `length_lpar_String_rpar_`NetFile << Net -- see [NetFile](../../Core/type/NetFile.md)pad(Net, ZZ) -- see [pad](../../Core/function/pad.md)pad(ZZ, Net) -- see [pad](../../Core/function/pad.md)File << Net -- see `printing_spc_to_spc_a_spc_file`unstack(Net) -- see [unstack](../../Core/function/unstack.md)`width_lpar_Net_rpar_`For the programmerThe object [Net](../../Core/type/Net.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor class [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `NetFile`

The class of all net files

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$NetFile`  

## Description

This class is experimental.  Net files are intended to supplant output files eventually.  Whereas a file is a stream of bytes, or in some non-unix operating systems, a sequence of lines each of which is a sequence of bytes, a net file is a sequence of lines, each of which is a net.  Each output line is assembled by joining nets one by one.### Methods that use an object of class NetFile: Methods that use an object of class NetFile: Manipulator NetFileNetFile << ManipulatorNetFile << NetNetFile << StringFor the programmerThe object [NetFile](../../Core/type/NetFile.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor class [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

name: OrderedMonoid
markdown:
# `OrderedMonoid`

The class of all ordered monoids

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$OrderedMonoid`  

## Description

An ordered monoid is a multiplicative monoid together with an ordering of its elements.  The ordering is required to be compatible with the multiplication in the sense that if x < y then x z < y z.  The class of all ordered monoids is [OrderedMonoid](../../Core/type/OrderedMonoid.md). The reason for making a separate class for ordered monoids is that monoid rings can be implemented more efficiently for them - an element of the monoid ring can be stored as a sorted list, each element of which is a pair consisting of an element of the monoid and a coefficient. See [PolynomialRing](../../Core/type/PolynomialRing.md). A free commutative ordered monoid can be created with [monoid](../../Core/function/monoid.md).### Types of ordered monoid: Types of ordered monoid:[GeneralOrderedMonoid](../../Core/type/GeneralOrderedMonoid.md)For the programmerThe object [OrderedMonoid](../../Core/type/OrderedMonoid.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [Monoid](../../Core/type/Monoid.md) < [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md) < [MutableHashTable](../../Core/type/MutableHashTable.md) < [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `ProductOrder`

Product ordering

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** SelfInitializingType  
**Aliases:** `Core$ProductOrder`  

## Description

`ProductOrder`{n1, ..., nr} -- an optional argument of [MonomialOrder](../../Core/object/MonomialOrder.md) to indicate that the monomial order is the product of r graded reverse lex orders, each with n1, n2, ..., nr variables. This syntax is left here for compatibility with previous Macaulay2 versions. The new syntax is `R = ZZ[a..e, MonomialOrder => {3,2}];`.


## Examples

```macaulay2
R = ZZ[a..e, MonomialOrder => ProductOrder {3,2}];
```
**Parent:** `BasicList`

# `Pseudocode`

The class of pseudocodes

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Pseudocode`  

## Description

The Macaulay2 interpreter compiles its language into pseudocode, which is evaluated later, step by step.  At each step, the evaluator is considering a pseudocode item.  These pseudocode items are normally not available to the user, but the internal function [pseudocode](../../Core/function/pseudocode.md) can convert a function closure to pseudocode and display their contents, the function [value](../../Core/function/value.md) can evaluate it (bindings of values to local symbols are enclosed with the pseudocode), the operator [===](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq__eq_.md) can be used for equality testing, and when the debugger is activated after an error, the variable [current](../../Core/object/current.md) contains the pseudocode step whose execution produced the error.### Types of Pseudocode: Types of `Pseudocode`: PseudocodeClosureMethods that use an object of class Pseudocode: code(Pseudocode) -- see [code](../../Core/function/code.md)locate(Pseudocode) -- see [locate](../../Core/function/locate.md)`toList_lpar_Pseudocode_rpar_``value_lpar_Pseudocode_rpar_`For the programmerThe object [Pseudocode](../../Core/type/Pseudocode.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor class [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `RingMap`

The class of all ring maps

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$RingMap`  

## Description

For an overview of ring maps, substitution of variables, and finding implicit equations of a set of polynomial or rational functions, see `substitution_spc_and_spc_maps_spc_between_spc_rings`. A ring map $F: R \rightarrow{} S$, where $R$ is a polynomial ring, is specified by giving the images in $S$ of the variables of $R$.  For a simple example, consider the following map.  Notice that, as is usual in Macaulay2, the target ring is given before the source. There are other ways to define ring maps.  See below. Apply matrices to ring elements, vectors, matrices, and ideals using usual function notation. The kernel of such ring maps are constructed with the aid of Gröbner bases. # `RR`

The class of all real numbers

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** InexactFieldFamily  
**Aliases:** `ℝ`, `Core$ℝ`, `Core$RR`  

## Description

A real number is entered as a sequence of decimal digits with a point.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision floating point number, using the `MPFR` library. The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using [precision](../../Core/function/precision.md). For real numbers, the functions [class](../../Core/function/class.md) and [ring](../../Core/function/ring.md) yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision. The precision can be specified on input by appending the letter `p` and a positive number. An optional exponent (for the power of ten to multiply by) can be specified on input by appending the letter `e` and a number. Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.)Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by [printingPrecision](../../Core/object/printingPrecision.md). The notion of equality tested by [==](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq_.md) amounts to equality of the internal binary digits. The notion of (strict) equality tested by [===](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq__eq_.md) also takes the precision into account. Perhaps surprisingly, the IEEE floating point standard also specifies that every number, including 0, has a sign bit, and strict equality testing takes it into account, as it must do, because some arithmetic and transcendental functions take it into account. Use [toExternalString](../../Core/function/toExternalString.md) to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before. Transcendental constants and functions are available to high precision, with [numeric](../../Core/function/numeric.md).### Functions and methods returning a real number: Functions and methods # `RRi`

The class of all real intervals

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** InexactFieldFamily  
**Aliases:** `Core$RRi`  

## Description

A real interval is entered as a pair of real numbers to the interval function.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision interval using the `MPFI` library. The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using [precision](../../Core/function/precision.md). For real intervals, the functions [class](../../Core/function/class.md) and [ring](../../Core/function/ring.md) yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision. The precision can be specified on input by specifying the precision of both input [RR](../../Core/type/RR.md) numbers. Alternatively, the precision can be specified by including the option `Precision`. Intervals can also be created using `span_lpar_Sequence_rpar_` to create the smallest interval containing the inputs. Operations using intervals are computed as sets so that the resulting intervals contain all possible outputs from pairs of points in input intervals. The notion of equality tested by [==](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq_.md) amounts to checking the equality of the endpoints of intervals. The notion of equality tested by [===](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq__eq_.md) takes into account the precision of the inputs as well. The notion of inequalities for intervals amounts to testing the inequality for all points in the intervals.  In particular, [<=](../../Core/operator/_lt__eq_.md) is not the same as [<](../../Core/operator/_lt_.md) or [==](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq_.md). Transcendental functions on intervals produce intervals containing the image of the function on the interval. Transcendental functions are available to high precision, with [numericInterval](../../Core/function/numericInterval.md). The left and right endpoints of an interval can be accessed with [left](../../Core/function/left.md) and [right](../../Core/function/right.md).  Similarly, the midpoint and the length of an interval can be found with [midpoint](../../Core/function/midpoint.md) and [diameter](../../Core/function/diameter.md).### Functions and methods returning # `Set`

The class of all sets

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Set`  

## Description

Elements of sets may be any immutable object, such as integers, ring elements and lists of such.  Ideals may also be elements of sets. Set operations, such as `isMember_lpar_Thing_cma_Set_rpar_`, `Set_spc__add__spc_Set`, `Set_spc__mul__spc_Set`, `Set_spc_-_spc_Set`, `Set_spc__mul__mul__spc_Set`, `VirtualTally_spc__pow__mul__mul__spc_ZZ`, and `isSubset_lpar_Set_cma_Set_rpar_` are available. For example,[Ideal](../../Core/type/Ideal.md) in Macaulay2 come equipped with a specific sequence of generators, so the following two ideals are not considered strictly equal, and thus the set containing them will appear to have two elements. However, if you [trim](../../Core/function/trim.md) the ideals, then the generating sets will be the same, and so the set containing them will have one element. A set is implemented as a [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md), whose keys are the elements of the set, and whose values are all 1.  In particular, this means that two objects are considered the same exactly when they are strictly equal, according to [===](../../Core/operator/_eq__eq__eq_.md).### Functions and methods returning a set: Functions and methods returning a set: children(Digraph, Thing) -- see `children`closedNeighborhood(Graph, Thing) -- see `closedNeighborhood`closure(Matroid, Set) -- see `closure`descendants(Digraph, Thing) -- see `descendants`forefathers(Digraph, Thing) -- see `forefathers`fundamentalCircuit(Matroid, List, Thing) -- see `fundamentalCircuit`fundamentalCircuit(Matroid, Set, ZZ) -- see `fundamentalCircuit`getSeparation(Matroid, ZZ) -- see `getSeparation`groundSet(Matroid) -- see `groundSet``intersect_lpar_Set_rpar_``intersect_lpar_Set_cma_Set_rpar_`Set * Set -- see `intersect_lpar_Set_cma_Set_rpar_`maxWeightBasis(Matroid, List) -- see `maxWeightBasis`neighbors(Graph, Thing) -- see `neighbors`nondescendants(Digraph, Thing) -- see `nondescendants`nonneighbors(Graph, Thing) -- see `nonneighbors`parents(Digraph, Thing) -- see `parents``select_lpar_Set_cma_Function_rpar_`select(ZZ, Set, Function) -- see `select_lpar_Set_cma_Function_rpar_`[set](../../Core/function/set.md)set(HashTable) -- see [set](../../Core/function/set.md)set(VisibleList) -- see [set](../../Core/function/set.md)`Set_spc__mul__mul__spc_Set``Set_spc_-_spc_Set`Set - # `String`

The class of all strings

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$String`  

## Description

A string is thing that contains a sequence of characters (bytes). A string is normally entered as a sequence of characters surrounded by quotation marks. Strings involving special characters can be entered by using the backslash as an escape character, see `_2qt_`.  For an alternate method of entering strings with fewer escape sequences, see `_slash__slash__slash_`. # `Symbol`

The class of all symbols

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Symbol`  

## Description

Symbols are entered as an alphabetic character followed by a sequence of alphanumeric characters; case is significant. The single symbol character ' is regarded as alphabetic, so that symbols such as `x'` may be used. Symbols are used as names for values to be preserved, as indeterminates in polynomial rings, and as keys in hash tables.  They may have global scope, meaning they are visible from every line of code, or local scope, with visibility restricted to a single file or function body.### Types of symbol: Types of symbol:[Keyword](../../Core/type/Keyword.md)Functions and methods returning a symbol:[global](../../Core/object/global.md)[local](../../Core/object/local.md)[symbol](../../Core/object/symbol.md)[threadLocal](../../Core/object/threadLocal.md)Methods that use a symbol: Symbol ? name: SymbolBody
markdown:
# `SymbolBody`

Symbol bodies

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$SymbolBody`  

## Description

A Macaulay2 symbol is much like a function closure, in that it comes equipped with a pointer to a frame that contains a value for it.  That value can be recovered with the function [value](../../Core/function/value.md), as follows. The two symbols created in the example above have something in common -- they are created by the same bit of code (the function `f`), but they have different values. To allow the user to determine whether two symbols are created by the same bit of code, Macaulay2 has the notion of symbol body, which parallel to the notion of function body.  It's essentially the symbol, but without the pointer to the frame that contains the value. All such symbol bodies are members of the class `SymbolBody`.


## Examples

```macaulay2
f = x -> symbol x
```
```
o1 = f
o1 : FunctionClosure
```
```macaulay2
s = f 1
```
```
o2 = x
o2 : Symbol
```
```macaulay2
t = f 2
```
```
o3 = x
o3 : Symbol
```
```macaulay2
value s
```
```
o4 = 1
```
```macaulay2
value t
```
```
o5 = 2
```
```macaulay2
symbolBody s
```
```
o6 = x
o6 : SymbolBody
```
```macaulay2
symbolBody t
```
```
o7 = x
o7 : SymbolBody
```
```macaulay2
symbolBody s === symbolBody t
```
```
o8 = true
```
```macaulay2
class symbolBody s
```
```
o9 = SymbolBody
o9 : Type
```
**Parent:** `Thing`

When an integer is not provided, this returns all the tests for the given package.  The position of each element would be passed as the first argument of [check](../../Core/function/check.md) to run the test. Each value is a `TestInput` object.  These are printed with the location of the file so that you may quickly jump to the source code of the test when using Emacs. If the test number is also provided, then the corresponding `TestInput` object is returned. The [locate](../../Core/function/locate.md) and [code](../../Core/function/code.md) functions do the expected thing when given a `TestInput` object. Passing only the key of the desired test to [code](../../Core/function/code.md) is supported as well. You may also pass a `TestInput` object to [edit](../../Core/function/edit.md) to open the code in your favorite editor.### Methods that use a test input: Methods that use a test input: capture(TestInput) -- see [capture](../../Core/function/capture.md)check(TestInput) -- see [check](../../Core/function/check.md)code(TestInput)locate(TestInput)For the programmerThe object [TestInput](../../Core/type/TestInput.md) is a [SelfInitializingType](../../Core/type/SelfInitializingType.md), with ancestor classes [HashTable](../../Core/type/HashTable.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `Time`

The class of all timing results

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$Time`  

## Description

`Time` is the class of all timing results.  Each timing result is a [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md) of the form `{t, v}`, where `t` is the number of seconds of cpu time used, and `v` is the value of the expression.### Functions and methods returning a timing result: Functions and methods returning a timing result:[elapsedTiming](../../Core/object/elapsedTiming.md)[timing](../../Core/object/timing.md)For the programmerThe object [Time](../../Core/type/Time.md) is a [Type](../../Core/type/Type.md), with ancestor classes [BasicList](../../Core/type/BasicList.md) < [Thing](../../Core/type/Thing.md).

# `WrapperType`

A class of lists with abbreviated constructors

**Package:** Core  
**Class:** Type  
**Aliases:** `Core$WrapperType`  

## Description

These are the types `X` of lists that can be constructed by expressions of the form `X {a, b, c,...}`, or, for lists of length one, by an expression of the form `X a`.
